title: The listening retreat
summary: An intimate cinema concept. Tactile timber, deliberate placement, and a little less distraction.
challenge: Hard, parallel surfaces can blur dialogue and create uneven bass across the seats. This sample brief explores a room that needs clarity without losing its warmth.
approach: Start with the seating and speaker layout, then treat first reflections with broadband absorption. Use slatted treatment as a visual rhythm, while reserving space for deeper low-frequency control after measurement.
outcome: Concept only: a coordinated palette of natural oak and charcoal felt. No installation or measured acoustic result is claimed. Final placement would follow an on-site assessment.

title: A room for the record
summary: A compact studio concept that balances a focused mix position with space to create.
challenge: In small studios, strong early reflections and low-frequency room modes can make mix decisions unreliable. The sample brief prioritises a symmetrical listening position.
approach: Place broadband panels at the side-wall reflection points and plan a safely supported ceiling cloud. Allocate corners for deep absorption. Check speaker and listener positions with measurements before choosing any tuned traps.
outcome: Concept only: a starting treatment plan, not a completed installation. Listen and measure again after installation before adding diffusion or committing to full coverage.

title: Space to think
summary: A workplace concept where a conversation does not have to compete with the room.
challenge: Glass, hard floors and large tables can prolong speech reverberation. This illustrative meeting-room brief aims for easier conversation and more intelligible video calls.
approach: Distribute absorption over available walls rather than concentrating it in one corner. A ceiling treatment can be useful where walls are mostly glazed. Keep ventilation, lighting and access clear.
outcome: Concept only: a calm material direction and a preliminary acoustic approach. Speech privacy between rooms would need separate consideration of doors, partitions and flanking paths.
